entities.note: Introduced the seven-inch 45 rpm record in 1949.
The seven-inch 45 rpm record: lower-cost, youth-accessible hit-song object. Price point in 1960s–70s Black Southern stores ~$0.50–$1.
RCA's 45 rpm record player/changer, demonstrated by NBC's Arthur Fiedler in 1949; the 45's dedicated domestic playback device.
The long-playing record album: higher-cost object (~$5–$7 in 1960s–70s Black Southern stores).
Southern record store described by an oral-history respondent as 'the place to be.' Location/state not established in the reporting; treat as comparative evidence.
George's Music Room, Chicago record store (North Lawndale, Roosevelt Road); owned/renamed by George Daniels 1969; closed 2010.
George Xavier Daniels (b. 1946), Chicago record-store owner; interviewed by The HistoryMakers 2007-04-23.
Importes Etc., Chicago record store supplying imports and recommendations to early house DJs.
Dr. Wax records; Hyde Park origins reported 1984 (provisional); Evanston branch customer evidence 2006–2008.
Farley Keith, early Chicago house DJ; recalled an import selling 1,000 copies in two weeks at Importes Etc.
Vince Lawrence, Chicago house DJ; recalled basement-party economy ($2 admission, $0.50 soda).
The HistoryMakers — African American video oral-history archive; holds the 2007 George Daniels interview.
Smithsonian National Museum of African American History and Culture; 2022 institutional synthesis on neighborhood record stores.
Source institution for sourced visuals (FSA/OWI and U.S. News & World Report collections).
NBC Radio/NBC — employer of Arthur Fiedler, who demonstrated RCA's 45 rpm player in a 1949 public-domain press photograph. Provenance-verified edge actor.
